questions.prompt: Which change reduces input tokens without removing the context needed to answer a customer?
options: Include the entire knowledge base in every request
Retrieve only relevant articles and the current customer's order data
Remove all context and let the model guess
Increase the maximum output tokens
questions.takeaway: You learned to send the right context, not all the context. Targeted retrieval and customer-scoped data reduce token cost while preserving answer quality.

questions.prompt: How should you arrange a prompt to make provider-side prefix caching more effective?
options: Put timestamps and changing order data first
Randomize the instructions on every request
Keep stable instructions at the beginning and put dynamic data later
Assume prompt caching eliminates all model charges
questions.takeaway: You learned that stable prefixes make prompt reuse possible. Prompt caching discounts reusable input; response caching can avoid a model call entirely when reuse is safe.

questions.prompt: What is the best way to decide whether a cheaper or open-weight model is a good replacement?
options: Compare cost per successful answer on the same workload while meeting the quality bar
Choose the model with the lowest advertised token price without testing
Compare only one easy question
Assume self-hosted models have no infrastructure cost
questions.takeaway: You learned to measure value, not just token price. Compare models on the same workload, include hosting costs where relevant, and keep quality at or above the 85% bar.

questions.prompt: Which routing strategy balances cost and answer quality?
options: Send every request to Premium
Send every request to Economy and never escalate
Retry every failed request forever
Use Economy for simple requests, Balanced for standard ones, and Premium for complex requests, with bounded escalation
questions.takeaway: You learned to match model capability to task difficulty. Routing and bounded escalation reserve expensive capacity for the requests that actually need it.

questions.prompt: A strategy is very cheap but answers only 78% of the full workload correctly. Is it a valid winning run?
options: Yes, because the lowest total spend always wins
No, it must meet at least 85% quality on the full 100-question workload before cost per success is ranked
Yes, if its latency is low enough
Yes, if it passes a smaller sample of easy questions
questions.takeaway: You learned to optimize cost per successful answer under a quality constraint. Savings only count when the full workload still meets the agreed quality bar.
